title: AegisBid Omega
subtitle: System implementation, issue resolution and measured limits

blocks.text:
50,000-bidder capacity: not yet reliably demonstrated.
Two historical HTTP-only runs passed. Later configurations failed the deadline target. A successful individual run does not certify the current system.

blocks.text: The decision contract

POST /v1/auctions/{id}/bids carries request_id and amount_cents. QUEUED means committed intake awaiting a decision. ACCEPTED means the price rule passed; final winners are selected later. REJECTED and CLOSED are terminal. HTTP 202 denotes pending intake; HTTP 200 denotes a final result. Retrying the same UUID must retain one business effect.
Authority and release boundary

PostgreSQL decides bids. NATS journals commands; workers also reconcile SQL pending rows. Go live updates are projections, not acceptance decisions. The latest scale layout separates Go admission and fanout services. Phase 13 remains unmerged because repeatable current-layout capacity is unresolved.

Solid arrows show processing; the dashed path reconciles SQL without broker delivery. Gold/green paths show isolated recovery. Late requests receive CLOSED receipts. Physical multi-zone deployment remains pending.
1. Concurrent price races and money accuracy

Issue: concurrent read/modify/write logic can accept conflicting offers. Change: the auction row serializes decision batches; money uses BIGINT cents. The required amount is max(reserve, current high + increment). Two equal-price offers cannot both advance the high. Check: PostgreSQL race tests and independent ledger replay verify outcomes and amounts.
2. Duplicate effects after retries or uncertain responses

Issue: clients may retry after losing an HTTP response or broker ACK. Change: a global request UUID binds one immutable bidder/auction/amount tuple. Changed payloads return 409; terminal retries reuse the original decision. Unique decision keys prevent a second effect. Check: concurrent retries and owner-history checks verify one request and one final outcome.
3. Late requests remained queued after final close

Cause: intake previously created QUEUED records while reconciliation scanned OPEN auctions only. Fix: a new late UUID now receives a CLOSED admission receipt with a reason/time, outside the sealed bidding ledger. Existing UUIDs retain their earlier result. Legacy stranded rows are repaired. Check: API/database tests verify final history and unchanged winners/anchor.
4. Parallel admission without losing sequence order

Change: sorted UUID locks prevent payload conflicts. A short reservation lock allocates sequence ranges; shared intake locks permit parallel inserts. Before selecting work, the worker takes an exclusive intake barrier so an uncommitted lower sequence cannot be overtaken. Sequence gaps are allowed; decision order stays increasing.

A new worker boot uses a new holder and a five-second lease with increasing epoch. Stale workers are fenced. Crash-before-commit rolls back the batch; redelivery after commit reuses terminal states. Close drains eligible pending work, then selects at most stock distinct offers by amount descending and decision sequence ascending.

pages.title: Performance issues: changes and open work

blocks.text: Implemented optimizations are not a capacity guarantee. Functional checks passed, but later full-load runs regressed. The remaining performance cause has not been isolated.
1. Distinct-user authentication was serialized

Cause: a global Go cache mutex covered upstream HTTP verification. Change: network calls run outside that mutex; identical sessions share a per-token flight, while up to 256 distinct verifications can proceed concurrently. A 30-second socket-auth cache reduces repeat work. Check: Go concurrency and race tests.
2. Per-request dispatch and database overhead

Changes: pure ASGI middleware, Linux uvloop, grouped identity lookup and bounded Go ingress. Groups hold at most 512 bids, collect for at most 100 ms and allow eight in-flight RPCs per auction. FastAPI still verifies every real JWT and role. Connection pools are bounded to 1..16 per process/DSN.
3. Publication and notification contention

Change: command_queue stores broker publication metadata separately from queued business rows. Up to 512 decisions commit together; each keeps its own result and hash event, while one outbox row names the latest batch version. This reduces repeated updates without discarding bid history.
4. The failure test also restarted migrations

Evidence: PostgreSQL logs showed migration DDL deadlocking with admissions after a Compose worker restart reran dependencies. Correction: restart only the recorded worker container and require the migration start timestamp to remain unchanged. This repaired test isolation; it did not resolve the remaining throughput gap.
5. Live updates plus bidding remain unresolved

Separate Go admission/live services, more live heap headroom and a two-second scale snapshot tick were attempted. Latest eligible counts were 42,794 for HTTP-only and 30,782 with 50,000 live sockets. Both missed the final-window gate. These changes remain experimental; the report does not label this issue solved.

pages.title: API roles, security and independent audit

rows: Submit integer-cent bids; resolve /v1/bid-requests/{id}; view own history, reasons and winners.
Create/schedule auctions with stock and price rules; close only owned auctions.
Inspect rates, queues, leases, backups and incidents; use explicitly enabled local chaos controls.
Retrieve sanitized evidence; independently verify event order, rules, hashes and allocation.

blocks.text: Identity and request protection

Passwords use salted scrypt (N=16,384, r=8, p=1). Four-hour HS256 sessions require subject, issuer and expiry. Cookies are HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict and Secure in production. Public bid bodies cannot supply bidder identity. Origin checks and owner/role checks protect writes and history. The hidden batch endpoint requires an independent service key before parsing, then verifies every session and role.
Auction Black Box / BidDNA verification

H_i = SHA256(ASCII(previous hex hash) || canonical_JSON(event))
canonical JSON: sorted keys, compact separators, ASCII escaping
signature = Ed25519(canonical unsigned export manifest)

A repeatable-read export fixes auction rules, ordered events, winners, version and terminal anchor. The independent verifier recomputes price progression, hashes, unique requests, stock bounds, close placement and winners. Altered evidence fails; unsigned evidence is INCOMPLETE. A trusted public key must be pinned separately. Receipts reference event hashes; they are not independent per-bid signatures. SQL storage is tamper-evident relative to trusted evidence, not WORM.
Operations and bounded live delivery

Go shares prepared frames with one replaceable pending snapshot per client; defaults cap sockets at 60,000 total/per auction and ten per user. Prometheus/Grafana expose SQL queues, latency and gateway signals. Test-only chaos requires an explicit flag; legacy restart/disconnect actions target the API service. Quotas are process-local; fleet-wide controls and pre-warming remain pending. The baseline comparison is an in-memory race model, not a legacy-system benchmark.
1. Database and broker failure

CloudNativePG configures three PostgreSQL instances with ANY 1 synchronous standby acknowledgment, failover quorum and isolation checks. NATS uses three file-backed replicas with authenticated TLS. SQL reconciliation recovers unpublished commands. An actual kind primary-node loss preserved three decisions and promoted a standby in 67.21 s. Its zone labels were simulated; this is not a physical zone or 50k-load database-failure proof.
2. Bacula backup and isolated restore

Director schedules -> File Daemon reads prepared artifacts
Storage Daemon writes media -> PostgreSQL Catalog indexes jobs

A shared exported SQL snapshot feeds pg_dump and a checksum/count manifest. Bacula backup/restore jobs completed with T status. Alternate-path restoration imported a fresh database and verified 20 decisions, 21 events and three winners in 1.25 s. A JSON/HTML restore certificate records verification. Live authority is never overwritten by the sandbox restore.
3. Physical point-in-time recovery

pg_basebackup and pg_verifybackup establish the base; archived WAL recovers a named/time target using recovery.signal. WAL publication uses temporary copy, fsync and atomic publication. A local drill recovered two decisions where the base contained one, matching the anchor in 3.12 s. Barman remote WAL resources are configured; continuous production offsite PITR/RPO is not yet demonstrated.
4. Protected remote copies

S3 artifacts use AES-256-GCM with object-key associated data, exact VersionIds and an encrypted index published last. A real Singapore restore verified a 20-decision dataset in 1.97 s, plus encryption, 30-day COMPLIANCE retention and protected-version deletion denial. The bucket uses the configured account; independent backup-account administration remains unproven.

Deployment boundary: three-zone EKS, zone placement, TLS and backup templates were validated, but EKS was not launched. Small controlled restore timers exclude full-site reconstruction. Catalog/configuration and decryption/signing keys also require independent recovery.

pages.title: Results: why PASS and FAIL coexist

blocks.text: PASS describes one recorded run, not every version. The successful historical HTTP runs used an earlier configuration. Later tested layouts regressed. Reliable current-layout 50k capacity remains unproven.
What failed in the latest trials?

The latest HTTP trial stored all 50,000 requests, but 7,206 received SQL admission timestamps after cutoff and were CLOSED; only 42,794 were eligible. With live feeds, 19,218 were late and only 30,782 were eligible. Request errors were zero, and both recorded correctness gates passed. The failed requirement was timely bidding. These are real performance failures, so they remain FAIL.
What did the historical passes prove?

All 50,000 original requests were matched to signed events; 20 winners replayed correctly. The worker trial confirmed SIGKILL/exit 137, checkpoint preservation and epoch 1 to 2 with stale-holder fencing. Queued work drained after cutoff. This proves those recorded runs; it does not show all decisions finished inside ten seconds.
Measurement scope and reproducibility

One auction used stock 20, reserve 10,000 cents and increment 10. Five generators offered one bid per distinct user over nine seconds, with at most 5,120 pooled HTTP connections on one 12-CPU / 7.46-GiB host. Sessions were pre-issued; login throughput and 50,000 simultaneous transactions were not measured. SQL timestamps occur inside transactions; exact commit visibility was not measured.

Evidence: docs/bidding-proof.md and docs/evidence/bidding-index.json list full IDs, configurations and replay commands. Historical baseline: f607529; latest tested: 9474f91. Repeatable 50k, physical multi-zone operation and full-site guarantees remain unproven.
